vignette:
Leilani was seventeen when she watched Koa slip on the slick deck and disappear into the churning grey water. She had been coiling a line nearby; she heard his shout, the heavy splash, then the frantic footsteps of the crew running past her. She froze, the rope slack in her hands. By the time someone threw a buoy, he was gone. In the weeks afterward, she told herself she should have thrown the line faster, should have yelled sooner-the thought coiled in her chest like a knot she could not loosen. She had failed to protect him, and that failure became a fixed fact she carried into every quiet moment. Carrying that belief-that she was someone who froze when it mattered-kept dragging her back to the moment itself, replaying the splash and the shouts as if she needed to find where she had gone wrong.

Now, two years later, the memory forces its way into her mind without warning. Sometimes she feels the full, choking intensity of the panic without any clear image-just the sensation of standing frozen on the deck, the guilt flooding her before she even knows why. At other times, the sound of footsteps behind her on the dock is enough to pull the scene back: the splash, the shouts, the way her body locked up. When she hears footsteps nearby, her whole system jerks into alertness before she can think-her body reacts to danger before her mind catches up, and then the memory arrives, sharp and unwanted. With each footstep, the thought came with it, quiet and certain: This is your fault. You should have moved faster. You failed him. Even the creak of a bicycle wheel near the harbour can do it, the high-pitched ring slicing through her day and landing her right back on that boat. After that happened once, she started taking a longer route to work that avoided the harbour entirely-adding twenty minutes each way was better than risking the sound that undid her. She also threw herself into double shifts the next day, working until her hands blistered, because stopping meant the feeling might come back.

Leilani learned early that keeping busy kept the memories at bay. She works double shifts on the fishing boat, hauling nets until her arms ache, staying out as long as the captain allows. At home, she spends hours scrolling through her phone, losing herself in games and videos rather than sitting still with her thoughts. The habit of filling every silent moment had made her hypervigilant to any sound that might break through; her ears were always waiting, and so she noticed every creak and footstep that she might have missed before. She has also avoided sex with her boyfriend, Mateo, for months-the closeness, the vulnerability, feels dangerous. She tells herself she is just tired, but she knows the real reason: any moment of quiet feels like a trap where the guilt can find her. The more she works, the more her mind seems to push back, the memories breaking through in flashes when she finally stops. She has come to believe that her body is an enemy, that it keeps reacting as if she is still in danger even when she is safe-and that reaction itself confirms the danger is still real. Because she never let herself stay still long enough to discover that nothing bad would happen, her nervous system never received the proof it needed-the threat remained as high as the day Koa went under, locked in place by the very strategies meant to contain it.

That fear has shaped everything. When something takes longer than expected-a net tangled, a boat delayed-she immediately assumes something bad is happening. Her concentration slips constantly; she loses track of conversations, misplaces gear, and Mateo has started to ask what is wrong. She cannot tell him that she is terrified of her own anger, of losing control and doing something terrible. That appraisal sits underneath everything: the guilt about Koa, the fear that she is capable of rage she cannot contain, the certainty that her body is betraying her.

The causal loops tighten around her. A trigger like footsteps brings the memory, and the memory reinforces her guilt, which makes her more sensitive to footsteps the next time. Her overwork drains her, which paradoxically makes the memories louder, which strengthens her belief that she cannot face them. Even her avoidance of sex-a strategy meant to keep her safe-feeds her sense of failure, as though she is failing Mateo the way she failed Koa. She is constantly scanning for threats, and the threat monitoring makes her notice triggers she might otherwise miss.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was an evening last month when Mateo asked her to talk, and she found herself on the floor, sobbing, unable to explain why. She is most afraid that if she lets the memories come freely, she will break apart-or that she will discover she is exactly as dangerous as she fears. But she is also tired of working herself to the bone and still waking up with the splash in her ears. She wants to know if her body can ever feel safe again.

violations.explanation: No paragraph shows that triggers (e.g., footsteps) cause Leilani to engage in maladaptive strategies like overwork or avoidance.
No paragraph shows that triggers directly cause negative appraisals (e.g., guilt or self-blame); instead, triggers lead to memory which then leads to appraisals.
No paragraph shows that negative appraisals (e.g., guilt) cause the trauma memory to intrude; the causal direction is memory → appraisals.
No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies (e.g., overwork) cause an increased sensitivity to triggers.
No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance) cause a heightened sense of threat; strategies are driven by threat, not the reverse.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph shows that triggers (e.g., footsteps) cause Leilani to engage in maladaptive strategies like overwork or avoidance.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that triggers directly cause negative appraisals (e.g., guilt or self-blame); instead, triggers lead to memory which then leads to appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph shows that negative appraisals (e.g., guilt) cause the trauma memory to intrude; the causal direction is memory → appraisals.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies (e.g., overwork) cause an increased sensitivity to triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance) cause a heightened sense of threat; strategies are driven by threat, not the reverse.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
